query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn system was selected to reduce cost while retaining the mechanical performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi; prior work reported comparable or better mechanical properties after excluding Co. Research on FeNiCrMn has mainly addressed corrosion, while studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys examined dynamic responses under tension or compression, different temperatures and strain rates, compositional changes, and the presence of cracks or voids. Those studies established that dynamic properties are sensitive to loading regime and material condition, but their different chemistries and defect states do not identify what governs FeNiCrMn. Under the constraints of retaining the Co-free composition and its strength–ductility balance, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains the dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes? Define a controlled study capable of testing the hypothesis, its applicable boundaries, the prior findings that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In the Co‐free FeNiCrMn alloy, the dynamic mechanical behavior is controlled by a temperature- and strain-rate–dependent transition between dislocation slip and deformation twinning. At higher strain rates and lower temperatures, the lower dislocation mobility promotes the activation of deformation twinning, which effectively increases strain hardening and sustains the strength–ductility balance, whereas at higher temperatures and lower strain rates, dislocation slip dominates the plastic deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast, solidified Co‐free FeNiCrMn with a primarily single-phase (likely FCC) microstructure
generation.intervention: Apply uniaxial mechanical loading (tension/compression) over a range of strain rates (from quasi-static ~10^(-3) s^(-1) to dynamic ~10^(3) s^(-1)) and temperatures (from cryogenic to room and elevated temperatures).
generation.conditions: Temperature varied (e.g., cryogenic, room, elevated) and strain rates varied (quasi-static to dynamic conditions) with otherwise identical microstructural and chemical conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The relative activity of dislocation slip versus deformation twinning within the metastable FCC matrix
generation.mechanism: At higher strain rates and lower temperatures, limited dislocation mobility in the metastable structure leads to a higher propensity for deformation twinning, which acts as an effective strain-hardening mechanism. Conversely, at higher temperatures or lower strain rates, enhanced dislocation motion dominates the deformation process, resulting in different strain-rate sensitivities.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under dynamic (high strain rate) and/or low-temperature conditions, samples will exhibit increased twin density alongside elevated strain-hardening rates and a maintained strength–ductility balance compared to conditions where dislocation slip predominates. Mechanical testing should show a systematic shift in yield strength and strain-hardening rate reflecting this mechanism switch.
generation.baseline: Mechanical properties measured at room temperature with intermediate strain rate where neither mechanism is overwhelmingly dominant.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies across conditions where the microstructure is metastable and single-phased (as-cast solidified state). It may not extend to thermomechanically processed or precipitate-strengthened variants where additional phases or interfaces govern the response.
generation.uncertainty: The exact transition thresholds (temperature and strain rate) where twinning becomes dominant are not precisely known and may be sensitive to minor processing variations and initial defect states.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of as-cast FeNiCrMn samples and conduct a series of uniaxial tensile and compressive tests across a range of temperatures (e.g., cryogenic, room, and elevated) and strain rates (ranging from ~10^(-3) s^(-1) to ~10^(3) s^(-1)). Post-deformation, employ microstructural characterization techniques (e.g., transmission electron microscopy and electron-backscatter diffraction) to quantify twin density and dislocation structures.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the mechanical testing and microstructural analysis do not reveal a systematic increase in deformation twinning at lower temperatures and/or higher strain rates, or if the strain-hardening behavior and strength–ductility balance remain unchanged (indicating a persistent dominance of dislocation slip regardless of testing conditions), then the hypothesis is falsified.

Influence of ordered L12 precipitation on strain-rate dependent mechanical behavior in a eutectic high entropy alloy

Abstract: Recent studies indicate that eutectic high-entropy alloys can simultaneously possess high strength and high ductility, which have potential industrial applications. The present study focuses on Al0.7CoCrFeNi, a lamellar dual-phase (fcc + B2) precipitation-strengthenable eutectic high entropy alloy. This alloy exhibits an fcc + B2 (B2 with bcc nano-precipitates) microstructure resulting in a combination of the soft and ductile fcc phase together with hard B2 phase. Low temperature annealing leads to the precipitation of ordered L12 intermetallic precipitates within the fcc resulting in enhanced strength. The strengthening contribution due to fine scale L12 is modeled using Orowan dislocation bowing and by-pass mechanism. The alloy was tested under quasi-static (strain-rate = 10−3 s−1) tensile loading and dynamic (strain-rate = 103 s−1) compressive loading. Nanoindentation behavior of high entropy alloys with transformation-induced plasticity

Abstract: Nanoindentation of three metastable dual-phase high entropy alloys (HEAs) was performed to obtain their inherent elastoplastic deformation responses. Excellent combination of hardness and elastic modulus in as-cast condition confirmed that, their inherently higher strength compared to other HEAs reported in literature, can be attributed to alloy chemistry induced phase stability. Further, hardness of 8.28 GPa combined with modulus of 221.8 GPa was obtained in Fe-Mn-Co-Cr-Si-Cu HEA by annealing the as-cast material, which is the best hardness-modulus combination obtained to date in HEAs from nanoindentation. On the other hand, although Fe-Mn-Co-Cr-Si HEA showed lower hardness and modulus than Fe-Mn-Co-Cr-Si-Al and Fe-Mn-Co-Cr-Si-Cu HEAs, the former alloy exhibited the highest strain rate sensitivity, as determined from tests performed at five different strain rates.
